context.in_practice: On every route, setting text that uses plain \n line endings works and is saved with CRLF endings, matching the file. Routes 1, 2 and 4 behaved identically in every run: a value with mixed endings is accepted and saved with all-CRLF endings, and the history records the converted value. Only route 3 behaved differently: it refuses mixed endings with exit 3, and the file, the stored value and the history all stay as they were.
context.stakes: A system prompt kept in a separate file with Windows (CRLF) line endings is rewritten when you set it from the command line. What matters is whether a value with mixed line endings is saved with consistent CRLF endings or rejected outright, leaving the old prompt in place.
context.tradeoff: Routes 1, 2 and 4 accept any line endings and quietly convert them all to CRLF. Route 3 never changes your text without telling you, but it rejects values that mix line endings, so you have to clean those up yourself first.

plan_why: Sets a CRLF text include to multi-line values (plain LF, no trailing newline, already containing CRLF) to show whether the read-back check accepts the CRLF-converted write, rejects it, or never runs; also shows what lands in the file, what get returns and which history events are recorded.
